title: Gravitation
short_intro: Gravitation is the universal attractive interaction acting between all masses in the universe, described classically by Newton's law of universal gravitation and geometrically by Einstein's general theory of relativity. It governs the motion of planets, satellites, and projectiles, forming a foundational central force field in classical mechanics.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Newton's law of universal gravitation, acceleration due to gravity (g) and its variation with altitude, depth, and latitude, gravitational potential and field, Kepler's laws of planetary motion, escape velocity, and orbital velocity of satellites.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Gravitational potential and field due to extended bodies (spherical shells, solid spheres), gravitational self-energy, motion under central forces, reduction of two-body problem to equivalent one-body problem, reduced mass, and effective potential energy curves.

prerequisites: Vector calculus and resolution of forces
Newton's laws of motion and kinematics
Work, energy, and conservation laws (angular momentum and mechanical energy)

concept_notes.heading: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
bullets: Every particle attracts every other particle with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
The vector form is given by F<sub>12</sub> = -G(m<sub>1</sub>m<sub>2</sub>/r<sup>3</sup>) r<sub>12</sub>, where the negative sign signifies the attractive nature of the force.
It is a conservative, central force obeying the inverse-square law, making the total mechanical energy of bound systems conserved.

concept_notes.heading: Variation of Acceleration Due to Gravity (g)
bullets: Due to altitude (h): g' = g(1 - 2h/R) for h << R, showing that g decreases with height above the Earth's surface.
Due to depth (d): g' = g(1 - d/R) assuming a uniform density sphere, indicating that g decreases linearly toward the Earth's center.
Due to rotation (latitude lambda): g' = g - R omega<sup>2</sup> cos<sup>2</sup>(lambda), causing g to be minimum at the equator and maximum at the poles.

concept_notes.heading: Gravitational Field and Potential
bullets: Gravitational field E is the gravitational force experienced per unit test mass placed at that point, with units N/kg or m/s<sup>2</sup>.
Gravitational potential V at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a test mass from infinity to that point against the gravitational field.
The relation between field and potential is given by E = -grad(V), reflecting the conservative nature of the gravitational force.

concept_notes.heading: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion
bullets: First Law (Law of Orbits): All planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun located at one of the foci.
Second Law (Law of Areas): The line joining the planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time, a direct consequence of conservation of angular momentum.
Third Law (Law of Periods): The square of the time period of revolution of a planet is directly proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its elliptical orbit.

derivations.title: Variation of Gravitational Acceleration with Depth
derivations.conditions: Earth is assumed to be a uniform solid sphere of radius R and mass M.
steps: Consider a point at a depth d below the Earth's surface. The effective distance from the center is r = R - d.
The mass of the inner sphere contributing to the gravitational pull at depth d is M' = (4/3) pi r<sup>3</sup> rho, where rho = M / ((4/3) pi R<sup>3</sup>).
Substituting rho, we get M' = M (r / R)<sup>3</sup> = M ((R - d) / R)<sup>3</sup>.
The acceleration due to gravity at depth d is g' = G M' / r<sup>2</sup> = G (M ((R - d)/R)<sup>3</sup>) / (R - d)<sup>2</sup>.
Simplifying yields g' = (G M / R<sup>2</sup>)(1 - d/R) = g(1 - d/R).

derivations.title: Escape Velocity from Earth's Surface
derivations.conditions: Body of mass m projected from the surface of Earth of mass M and radius R to infinity.
steps: Total mechanical energy on the surface of Earth is E = Kinetic Energy + Potential Energy = (1/2)m v<sub>e</sub><sup>2</sup> - (G M m) / R.
At infinity, the minimum velocity required makes both final kinetic energy and potential energy zero, so E = 0.
Applying conservation of mechanical energy: (1/2)m v<sub>e</sub><sup>2</sup> - (G M m) / R = 0.
Solving for v<sub>e</sub> gives v<sub>e</sub><sup>2</sup> = 2 G M / R.
Using g = G M / R<sup>2</sup>, substitute G M = g R<sup>2</sup> to obtain v<sub>e</sub> = sqrt(2 g R).

formula_sheet.conditions: Outside a spherically symmetric mass distribution, reference at infinity

formula_sheet.conditions: From the surface of a planet

graphs_and_experiments.title: Variation of g with Distance from Center (r)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A graph with r on the x-axis and g on the y-axis. For r < R, a straight line passing through the origin (g proportional to r). For r > R, a curve falling off as 1/r<sup>2</sup>.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that gravity increases linearly from the center to the surface, reaches a maximum at R, and then decreases inversely with the square of the distance outside.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in conceptual MCQs comparing g at internal points versus external points.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Effective Potential Energy Curve for Central Forces
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of U_eff(r) = L^2 / (2 m r^2) - G M m / r against radial distance r, showing a potential well with a minimum.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The minimum of the effective potential corresponds to a stable circular orbit where the centrifugal repulsive term balances the gravitational attractive term.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in PGT level problems to determine turning points, circular orbit radii, and stability.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Cavendish Experiment Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A torsion balance with two small lead spheres at the ends of a light rod suspended by a fine fiber, with two large lead spheres brought near them.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the weak gravitational attraction between laboratory-scale masses and is used to measure the universal gravitational constant G.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested as a conceptual question regarding the experimental determination of G.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the height above the Earth's surface at which the acceleration due to gravity drops to 36% of its value on the surface. (Radius of Earth R = 6400 km)
solution_steps: Formula for gravity at height h: g' = g (R / (R + h))^2.
Take square root on both sides: 0.6 = R / (R + h).
Calculate numerical value: h = (2/3) * 6400 km = 4266.67 km.

solved_numericals.question: A particle of mass m is placed at the center of a thin spherical shell of mass M and radius R. What is the net gravitational force on the particle, and what is the work done in moving the particle from the center to a point at distance 2R?
solution_steps: By shell theorem, the gravitational field inside a uniform spherical shell is zero everywhere. Thus, the net force on the particle at the center is zero.
Gravitational potential at the center of the shell: V_center = -G M / R.
Gravitational potential at a distance r = 2R outside the shell: V_outside = -G M / (2R).
Work done by an external agent in moving the mass m from center to 2R is W = m (V_final - V_initial).
solved_numericals.answer: Force = 0, Work done = (G M m) / (2 R)

solved_numericals.question: Find the orbital velocity and time period of an artificial satellite revolving in a circular orbit at a height of 600 km above the Earth's surface. (Take R = 6400 km, g = 9.8 m/s^2)
solution_steps: Radius of orbit r = R + h = 6400 + 600 = 7000 km = 7 * 10^6 m.
Orbital velocity v_o = sqrt(G M / r) = sqrt(g R^2 / r).
Time period T = (2 pi r) / v_o.
Substitute values: T = (2 * 3.1416 * 7 * 10^6) / 7572 approx 5808 seconds approx 96.8 minutes.

assumptions_and_limitations: Newton's law assumes instantaneous action at a distance, which fails for high-speed gravitational interactions governed by general relativity (finite speed of gravity equal to light speed c).
Earth is treated as a spherically symmetric body of uniform or spherically stratified density in elementary problems, whereas actual Earth is an oblate spheroid (geoid).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Gravity is zero at the center of the Earth because you are equidistant from all sides.
common_misconceptions.correct: Gravity is zero at the center because the mass shells enclosing spheres of zero radius exert no net force, and symmetrical mass cancellation results in zero vector sum.
common_misconceptions.why: Vector addition of forces from all directions inside a symmetric hollow or solid distribution results in total cancellation.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Escape velocity depends on the mass of the escaping body.
common_misconceptions.correct: Escape velocity is independent of the mass of the projectile.
common_misconceptions.why: Mass m cancels out in the energy conservation equation equating kinetic energy to gravitational potential energy.

quick_revision: Gravitational force is always attractive, conservative, and central, obeying the inverse-square law.
Newton's Law of Gravitation: F = \frac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2}
